title: Portraits in Courage - Hurricane Matthew Rescue
description: Hurricane Matthew created some of the worst flooding in North Carolina state history. Three Airmen assisted off base with rescue efforts and were recognized at the Air Force level event Portraits In Courage for their life-saving actions.
keywords: Fire Department, fire emergency, 4th Fighter Wing, Seymour Johnson, heroic, Portraits in Courage, SJAFB, 4FW, Air Force Emergency Services, ceremony, AIr Force, base, Fire, United States, event, heroes, fire fighters, honor, military

transcript.text: - [Newscaster 1] Massive cleanup effort
from Hurricane Matthew, the deadly storm claiming
at least 900 lives in Haiti, and here in the U.S.,
at least 22 people have died.
[Newscaster 2] In North Carolina,
they are now facing devastating flooding.
- [Newscaster 3] More bad news for folks living here
in North Carolina.
The waters here are still rising.
- [Newscaster 4] With its last gasp,
Matthew pounded the Carolinas.
- [Newscaster 5] As the sun rises in North Carolina,
and the blue sky returns,
our state is facing major destruction,
and sadly, the loss of life.
- In October 2016, myself, Tech Sergeant Andrew Vaughan,
^Captain Eric Hahs, responded to the Wayne County
^Emergency Operation Center to assist them
^in the rescuing of victims during Hurricane Matthew.
^- That morning, we came in like any other shift.
^We knew there was going to be inclement weather
^coming in, but we didn't know how drastic
^it was going to be.
^- We were all here at the fire department,
^actually just kind of relaxing.
All of our gear was ready to go.
We were staged, prepared for receiving a call
of anything happening.
- As the day grew and grew, the rain became heavier
and heavier, and the water level started to go up.
The head guy at the EOC for Wayne County
called our fire department and asked for a team
to come assist him, rescue stranded victims.
- At that time, the water levels in the streets
had risen to a point that the police and fire
were unable to travel the streets any longer,
so they requested a crew onto one of our crash trucks.
The reason being is these crash trucks
are quite a bit heavier, quite a bit larger and taller,
and the air intakes and the exhausts are on top
of the vehicles, and that allows us to be able to drive
through the deeper waters and a little bit
of the flood waters.
- Once we received some of those missions,
at first it was just rescuing stranded people
that weren't in any danger, and, from there,
the EOC asked us if we could go to another location
where they figured that our crash vehicle
was the only vehicle that could get there,
and low and behold when we got there,
it was a swift-water rescue.
- We helped with their haul lines and rope systems.
There was a woman stuck in a tree
who was calling for help.
She kept saying that she was just going to let go,
and if that happened, she was just going to get swept away
from us and there was nothing we could do to stop it.
- Soon after we arrived, a tree snapped and actually struck
one of the rescuers, and he actually was knocked
out of the boat, so it turned into a little bit
of a situation where now we had to assist
with the rescue of one of the rescuers themselves.
- Immediately we were on the haul team.
We pulled back in the rescuers,
and we had to reevaluate the situation
and come up with a different game plan
to get the woman out of the water.
- We actually got a boat from the county
with a motor to set up so they could try to go out
and get this lady out of the tree.
Once that boat arrived, we tied it off with rope again,
and two of the dive team members got into the boat
and was able to maneuver to the lady and rescue her
off of the tree and get her to safety.
- Good evening ladies and gentlemen.
I want to welcome you to Portraits In Courage.
A special evening highlighting 49 remarkable airmen,
recognized for their extraordinary acts of courage
^in combat, on duty, at home station,
^and within their communities.
- The reason we were submitted for Portraits in Courage
was for our actions with the county swift-water
rescue team, and us wading through water
that was unknown and downed power lines,
gusts of winds over 60 miles an hour,
just a ton of unknown scenarios that we put ourselves in
to save the lives of others.
- It was a great honor.
It was an honor to be able to be called.
It's an honor to be able to help others
in the outside community, outside of the gates.
It was a wonderful feeling knowing that some lives
were saved that night.
- It really was an honor to meet all the individuals
and the teams there that were selected.
^From people were saving lives,
^whether it was during deployment, stateside...
^People going through adversity at home and abroad.
^- It was an absolute honor to be able to represent
Seymour Johnson at the Pentagon.
It was just a privilege to be able to put ourselves
with those individuals and know that we have put a part
in saving the lives of people
and also to keep the mission going
as strong as the mission goes in today's Air Force.
(subtle, thoughtful instrumental)
